items.title: Advancing Spatial Pattern Integration in Species Distribution Modelling With Computer Vision: How Grain Size and Extent Concepts Shape Predictions of Emerging Aquatic Insects
items.abstract: Capturing spatial patterns in ecology necessitates jointly accounting for the concepts of grain size (i.e., the spatial resolution of the input data) and extent (i.e., the area covered by the input data). Species distribution models (SDMs) that rely on traditional machine learning models (e.g., Random Forest, MaxEnt) only integrate the grain size through environmental variables derived from raster data. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of Deep SDMs. Unlike traditional SDMs, Deep SDMs directly process image windows representing landscape context. Therefore, they can manipulate both the grain size and extent, through the spatial resolution and size of the windows, respectively. This study evaluates how grain size and window extent affect Deep SDMs, and how grain size alters the importance of variables (i.e., pixels of the image windows). We used multispectral and LiDAR data from drone and satellite acquisitions, with spatial resolutions ranging from 31 cm to 10 m, and varied the window extent between 40 m and 100 m. Grad-CAM was used to assess the importance of variables for each data type and measure their spatial agreement. As a case study, the terrestrial distribution of Plecoptera and Trichoptera, two orders of emerging aquatic insects with contrasting dispersal capacities, was predicted. Results demonstrated the capacity of Deep SDMs to integrate both the grain size and extent. They highlighted substantial variations in performance depending on the grain size (up to 0.26 AUC) and on the extent (up to 0.16 AUC). In particular, the best predictions were obtained using 2.5 m multispectral data at a 40 m extent for Plecoptera (limited dispersers), and the same multispectral resolution combined with LiDAR at a 100 m extent for Trichoptera (greater dispersers). Results also showed a moderate but notable change in variable importance with different grain sizes. Given the growing availability of remote sensing products, our findings advocate for systematic analysis of grain size and extent with Deep SDMs. This is essential to efficiently capture spatio-ecological patterns and to better understand the studied species. Datasets and code are publicly available 1 .

items.title: Projected Climate‐Induced Range Dynamics of Alburnoides Species in Anatolia Using an Ensemble Species Distribution Model
items.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems harbour a substantial proportion of global biodiversity yet face intense pressure from multiple stressors. Historical models indicate that Türkiye has served as a crucial hub of fish diversification since the Late Miocene, although projections suggest that freshwater biodiversity faces escalating threats. This study investigates the past, present and future distribution dynamics of 14 species belonging to the Alburnoides genus in Türkiye using an ensemble species distribution modelling (SDM) approach. Habitat suitability was assessed under present conditions and future climate scenarios (SSP1–2.6 and SSP5–8.5) by integrating species records with climatic, hydrological and environmental variables. The results show that temperature and precipitation are the dominant limiting factors determining habitat suitability for the genus Alburnoides , with species thriving in well‐oxygenated, rapidly flowing streams within a temperature range of 7°C–20°C. Future projections indicate a substantial contraction of suitable habitats across Türkiye, particularly under the high‐emission scenario (SSP5–8.5). However, a select few species are anticipated to experience range expansion as newly suitable habitats emerge under future climate scenarios. These findings highlight the necessity of formulating basin‐wide and climate change‐adaptive management methods for the preservation of biodiversity in Turkish inland water ecosystems.

items.title: Current and future climatic suitability of the cotton jassid, Amrasca biguttula in Togo under climate change: insights from ensemble species distribution models
items.abstract: Amrasca biguttula is an emerging pest of cotton and vegetable crops in West Africa, yet its spatial distribution and potential response to climate change remain poorly understood in Togo. This study assessed its current and future habitat suitability across Togo using an ensemble species distribution modelling approach to identify areas requiring priority surveillance. A total of 73 spatially independent occurrence records and 10 environmental predictors representing climatic and anthropogenic conditions were used to calibrate the models. The ensemble model showed high predictive performance (mean AUC = 0.963; TSS = 0.848). Current habitat suitability was highest in southern Togo, particularly in the Maritime Region and parts of the Plateaux Region, and decreased towards central and northern areas. Human footprint, precipitation of the driest month, isothermality and minimum temperature of the coldest month were among the most influential predictors. Host-crop-associated suitability was assessed in relation to the distribution and intensity of tomato, cotton and other vegetable production. Future projections under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 for 2041-2060 and 2061-2080 indicated more pronounced changes under SSP5-8.5, particularly during 2061-2080, with areas of both suitability expansion and contraction. Ensemble species distribution modelling provides a useful approach for identifying areas potentially at risk from A. biguttula under current and future climatic conditions. The resulting maps provide a spatial baseline for prioritizing pest surveillance and supporting climate-informed integrated pest management in Togo. Keywords: Spatial prediction, environmental niche models, pest management, surveillance, field survey.

items.title: Integrating land-use and climate connectivity to link protected areas at the country level
items.abstract: Context Ecological corridors that are high in biodiversity potential and stable under climate change are central to long-term conservation planning. Yet spatial prioritization frameworks rarely integrate land-use resistance and climate stability into a unified approach, limiting their operational value for landscape management and policy. Objectives We aimed to develop an ecological connectivity framework that jointly incorporates land-use resistance and climate stability to map linkages among protected areas, and to quantify and communicate methodological uncertainty arising from key parameterization choices. Methods We applied the framework to Portugal's terrestrial protected-area network. Using a full factorial design, we varied land-use resistance, climate resistance, and dispersal capacity across multiple weightings to generate optimized linkage solutions. Selection-frequency maps derived from these solutions fed a second optimization round, producing an ensemble connectivity solution and buffered corridors. Results Individual solutions covered 0.74% of Portugal's unprotected land; the ensemble covered 0.07%, rising to 2.3% after a 1 km buffer. Dispersal capacity parameterization introduced greater uncertainty in connectivity outcomes than land-use or climate resistance scores, suggesting it deserves particular attention in future studies. Protected areas in the Central–North region emerged as the most critical network hubs, with the highest centrality under both resistance gradients. The ensemble highlighted areas of high concordance across parameterizations, improving the robustness of spatial priorities. Conclusions Integrating land-use and climate resistance identifies corridors that are both functional and climate-resilient. Explicitly mapping uncertainty and producing ensemble-prioritized linkages improves the reliability of spatial recommendations, offering planners a practical tool for embedding connectivity targets into conservation and land management decisions.

items.title: Assessing the accuracy and stability of variable importance in species distribution modelling algorithms through sample perturbations
items.abstract: Variable importance derived from species distribution modelling (SDM) is widely used to identify key environmental drivers of species distributions. However, the reliability of these inferences has rarely been systematically evaluated, particularly with respect to their sensitivity to individual occurrences. Here, we used virtual species and developed a sample perturbations diagnostic framework, in which each occurrence was systematically removed (leave‐one‐out) to assess how small changes in the input data affect variable importance inference. Using this framework, we evaluated and compared ten SDM algorithms across multiple scenarios. We constructed a set of evaluation metrics to quantify both the accuracy of driver identification and the stability of permutation importance estimates, defined as their variability under sample perturbations. We further investigated the sample level mechanisms underlying instability. Our results showed that random forest (RF), gradient boosting machine (GBM), and maximum entropy (Maxent) achieved the best overall performance. RF exhibited the relatively high inferential accuracy and stability, but showed limited ability to differentiate the relative importance of environmental variables. GBM and Maxent achieved slightly lower accuracy than RF, but were more stable and effective for distinguishing the relative contributions of different variables. Instead, several algorithms displayed relatively high accuracy but were sensitive to sample perturbations. Scenario analyses indicated that stability generally increased under conditions of high sample sizes, low geographical sampling bias, and moderate prevalence. Highly influential occurrences were not necessarily associated with extreme environmental conditions. Removal experiments further demonstrated that variable importance inference in several algorithms was sensitive to a relatively small subset of occurrences, highlighting the disproportionate contribution of these occurrences. Overall, this study provides a sample level diagnostic framework for evaluating the reliability of variable importance in SDM, offering practical guidance for improving the interpretability of environmental driver inference in ecological research and conservation applications.

items.title: Mapping Biome Boundaries From Climate Patterns: A Machine Learning Framework
items.abstract: Aim To develop a climate‐based, probabilistic framework that maps global biomes as climatic domains and explicitly quantifies the spatial distribution and intensity of biome transition zones. Location Global terrestrial biomes. Methods We trained a probabilistic machine‐learning classifier linking biomes to multivariate climate space. We quantified biome ambiguity for each grid cell using Shannon entropy, identifying ecotones as regions where climate supports multiple biome outcomes, that is, high entropy. We applied the framework to present‐day climate and mid‐century climate projections to evaluate potential biome reorganization and ecotone shifts under climate change. Results The model reproduced the broad geographic distribution of major biomes, although spatially blocked validation revealed variation in geographic transferability among biome classes. High‐entropy zones form coherent transition belts that coincide with well‐known ecotones, including forest–savanna boundaries, desert margins, temperate forest–grassland transitions, and the boreal–tundra interface. Biome core regions show low entropy, whereas ecotones exhibit diffuse probability structure and heightened sensitivity to climatic variation. Projections of the model under mid‐century climatic conditions (2041–2060) identify spatially structured patterns of biome transitions, particularly shifts from tundra to boreal forest and from boreal to temperate systems, while also highlighting regions where uncertainty and model disagreement are greatest. Main Conclusions Mapping biomes in climate‐probability space reframes biome boundaries as spatially extended, permeable zones shaped by overlapping climatic regimes. By combining probabilistic classification with entropy‐based uncertainty quantification, our framework complements traditional biome maps by revealing the gradient structure and stability of biome transitions and by identifying where climatic change is most likely to drive ecological reorganization. The resulting transition and uncertainty surfaces offer globally comparable spatial layers for macroecology, biogeography, and evolutionary research, including studies linking ecotones to biodiversity patterns, trait turnover, and lineage diversification.

items.title: Dispersal Limitations Restrict Predicted Climate‐Driven Biodiversity Dynamics Across North America
items.abstract: Aim Species may not fully track shifting climatic conditions when dispersal is limited, yet how species‐specific dispersal constraints scale up to shape biodiversity redistribution across taxa remains unclear. We evaluated how dispersal limitation modifies projected biodiversity dynamics under climate change. Location North America. Time Period Contemporary to late 21st century. Major Taxa Studied Terrestrial vertebrates. Methods We developed species distribution models for 256 terrestrial vertebrate species spanning dispersal rates from 0 to ~100 km/year. We compared climate‐driven projections based on climatic suitability with projections incorporating species‐specific dispersal constraints. We further assessed how dispersal capacity influences habitat accessibility and projected overlap with major land‐cover categories and protected areas. Results Dispersal limitation substantially altered the magnitude and spatial structure of projected biodiversity change. Climate‐driven projections predicted increasing species richness and poleward range expansion, whereas dispersal‐limited projections suppressed leading‐edge expansion, amplified range contraction and generated extensive climatically suitable but inaccessible habitat. These effects intensified under stronger climate forcing and were most pronounced at high latitudes. Species with lower dispersal capacities experienced substantially greater mismatches between climatically suitable and accessible habitat. Dispersal limitation also altered projected landscape overlap: overlap with forests, wetlands, and protected areas increased under climate‐driven projections but declined when dispersal constraints were incorporated, whereas dispersal limitation attenuated projected increases or amplified projected declines in other landscape categories. Main Conclusions Species‐specific dispersal capacity acts as a biological filter on climate tracking, and climate‐driven projections may therefore overestimate species' ability to track environmental change. These species‐level constraints scale up to alter continental biodiversity redistribution and its spatial correspondence with different landscape types. Incorporating dispersal processes is therefore essential for projecting future biodiversity change and informing conservation planning.

items.title: Leveraging Species Associations Patterns of Macroalgae in Wrack to Predict Their Spatial Distribution
items.abstract: Aim Species associations are increasingly recognized as an effective way to improve species distribution model (SDM) predictions by integrating biotic and abiotic information that is difficult to measure in situ. This approach appears promising for monitoring communities where biodiversity and environmental data are sparse or limited. To evaluate its applicability to such communities and to test whether associations estimated in narrow spatial context can capture useful information and be transferred to predict spatial distributions across larger regions, we focused on macroalgal communities in beach wrack. Location France. Methods To estimate the information captured by macroalgae species associations, we assessed the predictive improvement they provide when added to models of increasing complexity using a random forest approach. We also examined how species traits influence association patterns among 58 species observed at 130 sites in Brittany, western France. Finally, we quantified the improvement in predictive performance when applying these associations to species distribution models across 402 sites along the French Atlantic coast. Results We found that species associations both complement and substitute remote sensing and fine‐scale habitat descriptors in predicting individual species distributions. Association patterns were related to certain macroalgae traits (e.g., buoyancy status, initial benthic habitats). They significantly improved large‐scale predictive performance, despite being derived from limited sample sizes and narrow spatial contexts, confirming that such associations capture more than initial or local environmental factors. Main Conclusions Using macroalgal communities in beach wrack, we illustrate that species associations can serve as alternative predictors for communities where biotic and abiotic data are scarce or hard to access. We also highlight their usefulness for predicting at broader spatial scales than those used for their estimation. Leveraging these associations offers promising tools to enhance spatial conservation planning, identify sampling biases and guide efficient surveys (e.g., in exotic or rare species of high conservation concern).
